newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says Palestinians delaying Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says Palestinians delaying Hebron deal.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday the PLO was delaying a deal on Israeli troop redeployment from Hebron confident Israel would be blamed for any foot-dragging.

"One of the reasons the Palestinian side is holding up its completion is that it assumes...any time the Arab side alleges there is a problem in moving forward, Israel's government will be blamed," Netanyahu said in a speech in Tel Aviv.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, ending three weeks of marathon mediation in a bid to nail down details of the long-delayed pullout from the West Bank town, left for Washington on Tuesday.
On Monday, the United States said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat alone could not be blamed for the failure so far to reach agreement.
"It's wrong and I think it's also not consistent with the facts to point at Chairman Arafat and say: 'He's the guy holding these talks up'," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"I would just look at both of them (Israelis and Palestinians) and say they're both responsible, and they're only going to get an agreement when both of them cross the line together," Burns told reporters in Washington.
Palestinian and Israeli officials said they would meet in Jerusalem on Tuesday to hash out remaining sticking points.
Arafat, in Oslo on the first leg of a three-day tour, said it was Israel that was keeping the deal from being struck.
"I am sorry to say that still the Israelis are making new conditions every day," Arafat said. He said agreement could still be reached on Hebron before U.S. elections on November 5.
But Israelis were pessimistic on chances of any progress before the return from Europe later this week of Arafat, who left for Norway on Monday.

Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh, saying the sides had been only "a number of hours" away from agreement, said he had "not heard of any serious explanation why this trip to Europe was more important than the need to reach agreement on Hebron".
Clinton dispatched Ross to the region in the wake of unprecedented Palestinian-Israeli gun battles last month that left scores dead in the West Bank and Gaza.
Violence erupted in a West Bank village on Tuesday after the funeral of a 10-year-old Palestinian boy who relatives said had been killed by a Jewish settler on Sunday.

About 50 masked mourners threw rocks at Israeli cars travelling on a road below used by Jewish settlers. Other mourners joined in and soldiers responded by firing live ammunition, rubber bullets and teargas, witnesses said.

"Get the Nazis out of our land," read one banner at the burial attended by 5,000 mourners who vowed to avenge the killing of Hilmi Shosha. Arab witnesses said a settler had beaten the boy unconsious on suspicion of throwing stones.
In a bid to lend fresh impetus to the Middle East peace process, Jordan's King Hussein visited Egypt on Tuesday for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns the Jewish state agreed to hand over to Palestinian self-rule.
Israel's previous Labour government agreed to a pullout from the violence-plagued town more than a year ago, but suspended the measure in response to a wave of Islamic suicide bombings.
Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to dictate new terms for the Hebron redeployment, delayed since March. PLO officials say they will brook no alterations to the original agreement.
Israel has said changes are needed to safeguard the 400 Jews who live and study under heavy army guard among 100,000 Arabs.
The differences centred on Israel's demand for the right to pursue militants into parts of Hebron it hands over, and what arms PLO police would be allowed to carry, Palestinians said.
